label: <DEL> delimiter step, stronger for long sequences and certain first tokens
explanation: Fires essentially only at the <DEL> delimiter step (t == L): 100% of activation mass is there, with 2 stray original-phase steps in the whole dev split. It never fires on original tokens or during the copy phase. It is active on about 65% of delimiter steps, and two things decide which ones. (1) Sequence length: the active rate at the delimiter climbs steadily with L (about 37% at L=3, 41% L=4, 49% L=5, 58% L=6, 68% L=7, 81% L=8, 92% L=9), and the share of activation mass grows with L too. (2) The first original token, which is the token to be output at this step: some first tokens give about 85-97% active delimiters (w, 0, i, u, q, 2, m, o, t, etc.), while others give only 23-35% (r, f, z, 3, h). Simple version: phase==1 has F1 0.785, recall about 1.0, precision 0.65. Adding the condition (first token in the high-rate set OR L>=7) gives dev F1 0.84 and mass recall 0.955. The top activations are long (L=8-9) sequences starting with w or 0.

issues: The factual claims check out on dev. 100% of activation mass falls at the delimiter step, with only 2 stray original-phase steps. The active rate at the delimiter is 0.37 at L=3, 0.49 at L=5, 0.68 at L=7 and 0.92 at L=9. By first token it is w 0.97, 0 0.95, r 0.23, f 0.27, z 0.30, 3 0.31, h 0.36. Test scores reproduce exactly: P 0.783, R 0.909, F1 0.841, mass recall 0.955.

Systematic omission: whether the unit fires depends on several positions in the sequence, not just the first token and L. The second original token, orig(1), matters almost as much as the first: w 0.84, 0 0.77, s 0.68, r 0.46, z 0.39, f 0.37.

The last original token (prev_tok at the delimiter) also moves the rate a lot, from about 0.47 (u) to 0.86 (r), and its preferences run roughly opposite to the first-token ones. As the last token, r is 0.86, f 0.83, s 0.83 and w 0.56. As the first token, r and f are low and w is high. The second-to-last token (prev2_tok) shows the same pattern (r/f/s about 0.81, w 0.60).

The test misses show this pattern. Missed activations are short sequences with an unfavourable first token but a favourable ending, e.g. 'h m r s', 'b n u j s', 'k l z', 'j e 1 n 2 p'. False positives are long sequences that start with low-rate tokens (z, f, r, h, v, y). The unit looks like a graded score built up over the whole sequence, which the OR-rule only approximates.
The label overclaims a little: 'certain first tokens' presents a single-position lookup as the token factor, when the first token is only the strongest of several position-dependent contributions.
skeptic.revised_label: The <DEL> delimiter step only, gated by a graded score that rises with sequence length L. Early tokens (first, second) push it up when they are w/0/i/u/q-like; the last tokens push it up when they are r/s/f-like.
